deed: Ruth Gruber escorts a thousand refugees from Italy to the United States on behalf of the Roosevelt administration
title: Ruth Gruber escorted about a thousand refugees from Italy to a haven in the United States, and they stayed there

trailer.text: Ruth Gruber was an American Jewish journalist and photographer, born in Brooklyn in 1911 to Jewish immigrant parents from Russia.
According to JWA, Secretary of the Interior Harold Ickes chose her to go on a secret mission and escort refugees to the United States.

The refugees arrived in New York harbor on August 3, 1944 and were given sanctuary on an old army base in Oswego, which, according to the National Park Service, was the only shelter in the United States for Jewish refugees who fled the Holocaust.
According to JTA, only a special directive by President Truman prevented their deportation at the end of 1945.
According to the National Park Service, they settled across the United States and became doctors, musicians and filmmakers.

paragraphs.text: The Johnson-Reed Act of 1924 sharply restricted immigration to the United States.
According to the National Park Service, until 1944 the United States government made no concerted effort to help Jews escape Nazi genocide.
According to NPS, during the first years of the war State Department officials purposely obstructed efforts to assist Jewish refugees.
These officials acted under the leadership of Assistant Secretary of State Breckinridge Long.
According to Aish, in 1944 refugees from Yugoslavia were streaming into Italy at a rate of 1,800 a week, and they were getting in the way of the American military.

stations.title: The Decision in the White House

paragraphs.text: According to NPS, in early 1944 employees at the Treasury Department persuaded President Roosevelt to try to help.
According to Aish, six days after Morgenthau's visit to the White House, Roosevelt created the War Refugee Board.
Gruber said that Roosevelt decided to open the gates of the United States and take in 1,000 war refugees.
According to the Times of Israel, Congress had set strict immigration quotas, and so Roosevelt used his executive authority and invited the refugees as his "guests".
According to the USHMM, on June 12, 1944 Roosevelt formally announced a "free port" for refugees at Fort Ontario in Oswego.
According to the Consider the Source website, the War Refugee Board set up the camp, and the War Relocation Authority managed daily life there.
Gruber was born on September 30, 1911, in Brooklyn.
The New York Times reported on the doctorate she received at a young age, and there are two versions of what it said.
According to the JWA Encyclopedia, Ickes selected Gruber to fly to Europe on a secret mission and escort the refugees to America.
Ickes told her she would be given the rank of "simulated general".
That way, if the Nazis captured her, they would be obliged to give her food and shelter.
According to Aish, Gruber told Ickes that someone had to be with the refugees on their journey and take their hand.
Gruber said that priority was given to those who had escaped from Nazi concentration camps and labor camps.
According to the Times of Israel, more than 3,000 people were applicants for the journey.
According to the Times of Israel, the refugees were forced to sign a document stating they would return to Europe at the end of the war, and they were not given legal status.
According to the Times of Israel, the refugees boarded the ship Henry Gibbins and set sail in July 1944.
According to Aish, the convoy set sail on July 20, 1944.
According to the Times of Israel, while the ship was sailing in the Mediterranean, 30 Nazi planes flew over it.
According to Aish, the captain of the Henry Gibbins released black smoke to camouflage the ship, and it was not attacked.
On the way, Gruber recorded the refugees' stories of how they had survived.
According to JTA, she spoke German and Yiddish, organized English lessons and cared for the seasick.
According to JTA, in the refugees' eyes she became a symbol of hope and salvation, and they called her "Mother Ruth".
In her book, Gruber told of a rabbi who conducted a service as the ship passed the Statue of Liberty.
According to JTA, the refugees sailed from Naples aboard the troopship Henry Gibbins.

On August 3, 1944 the refugees arrived in New York harbor, and from there they continued to a sanctuary on an old army base in Oswego.
According to the Consider the Source website, when they arrived at Fort Ontario they were faced with a six-foot barbed wire fence.
According to Aish, Oswego residents began passing milk and food through the fence, and the refugees calmed down.
According to the Forward, Ruth Gruber said that Doris Schechter entered kindergarten after a two-month quarantine.
According to NPS, the children rode buses to public schools in Oswego.
There are different versions about the adults' work.
The refugee Walter Greenberg said that he felt deceived and that he should have been free.
According to Aish, the refugee Maurice Kamhi said that the refugees were in a bubble of safety, and that no one was chasing them to death at every moment.
According to Aish, in April 1945 Gruber wrote a report about the camp and argued that its residents should be accepted.
According to JTA, only a special directive by President Truman prevented the refugees' deportation.
According to the Times of Israel, they were taken to Canada and given visas to the United States there.
According to the Times of Israel, President Truman's decision regarding the refugees is attributed to the work of the camp director, Dr. Joseph Smart, and to Eleanor Roosevelt, who took up the cause.
According to the USHMM, on September 20, 1944
According to NPS, the refugees settled across the United States and became doctors, musicians, hairdressers, therapists and filmmakers.
According to My Jewish Learning, Dr. Alex Margulis, born in Belgrade, Yugoslavia (1921), helped develop the CAT scan and the MRI.
At the 1984 reunion, Governor Mario Cuomo said that the refugees had repaid the state any debt they had.
According to JTA, many of those at the reunion again called Gruber "Mother Ruth".
According to the JWA Encyclopedia, the museum library in Oswego is named after Gruber.
The story was adapted into a television film titled Haven, which CBS aired in 2001.
According to the Forward, Gruber died on November 17, 2016, at age 105.
According to JWA, the actress Natasha Richardson played Ruth in the miniseries.
The camp was only a symbolic concession by Roosevelt, not a significant change in policy.
According to the Times of Israel, it was the only time the United States brought Jewish refugees en masse.
According to JWA, the story ended happily for the refugees, but at the expense of others waiting in displaced persons camps in Europe.
According to Aish, Dr. Shum of the Safe Haven Museum says that historians view the operation as an embarrassing chapter in American history.
Gruber said that a thousand refugees make up in some measure for the thousands who could have been saved.
According to JTA, until the end of her life she remained convinced that the United States could have saved many more refugees.

disagreements.question: When did Roosevelt decide, and when was the shelter established?

versions.says: According to Aish, Roosevelt created the War Refugee Board in January 1944, and the decision on the shelter became official several months later
According to the USHMM, Roosevelt formally announced the shelter on June 12, 1944
According to the Times of Israel, 982 refugees boarded the ship
According to JWA, Roosevelt planned to allow 984 refugees to stay until the end of hostilities

disagreements.question: How many of the refugees were Jewish?

versions.says: According to JTA, 872 were Jewish, and the rest were Catholic, Protestant, Greek Orthodox or born of mixed marriages
According to Aish, 874 of the 982 were Jewish
According to Consider the Source, 93% of the 982 refugees were Jewish, and of all the refugees, 187 were under the age of 16 and 116 were over the age of 60.

disagreements.question: How many ships were in the convoy?

versions.says: Gruber spoke of 29 ships, about 15 of them warships
According to Aish, 16 troop and cargo ships and 13 warships

disagreements.question: How long did the quarantine on entering the camp last?

versions.says: During the first month, the refugees were not permitted to leave the camp
According to the Forward, Ruth Gruber said that Doris Schechter went through a two-month quarantine.

disagreements.question: Were the adults allowed to work outside the camp?

versions.says: According to NPS, adults worked at the camp or in nearby Oswego
According to Consider the Source, they were generally not allowed to seek employment outside the camp
According to Aish, the adults could not obtain jobs

disagreements.question: When did the refugees receive visas?

versions.says: According to JTA, in January 1946 the first group, 98 refugees, received visas at Niagara in Canada
According to JTA, a directive by Truman prevented their deportation in December 1945
According to NPS, Truman ordered in 1946 that they receive visas

disagreements.question: The youngest PhD in the world, or only in Germany?

versions.says: According to the JWA Encyclopedia, the New York Times reported that at age 20 she was the youngest PhD in the world
According to the Times of Israel, the New York Times reported in 1932 that she was the youngest German Doctor of Philosophy, not the youngest in the world

claims.text: לפי NPS, פורט אונטריו שימש בשנים 1944–1946 כמקלט היחיד בארצות הברית לפליטים יהודים שברחו מהשואה.

claims.text: לפי JTA, רק הוראה מיוחדת של הנשיא טרומן מנעה את גירושם של הפליטים בדצמבר 1945.

claims.quote: They settled across the country, getting married, having families, and becoming doctors, musicians, hairdressers, therapists, and filmmakers.

claims.text: לפי ה-USHMM, ב-12 ביוני 1944 הכריז רוזוולט רשמית על תוכניתו ליצור "נמל חופשי" לפליטים בפורט אונטריו באוסוגו.
